1b:
**Sub-item 1b — "Answer incorrectly states that an exception cannot occur" (−2):**

Apply this deduction only when the answer denies that any exception can occur at this location at all — i.e., it tells the user the code is safe and no exception will be thrown there. Do not deduct if the answer affirms, anywhere, that an exception can occur in at least one scenario at this location; a scenario-specific denial does not trigger this deduction. For example, an answer that says a ClassCastException can occur when the lookup returns a Fragment of the wrong type, but also (wrongly) says that the fragment-not-found case is handled safely and would not throw, still satisfies this sub-item and gets no deduction here — that mistaken claim about the not-found scenario is penalized under sub-item 4b instead, not here. In short: deduct 2 points for a blanket denial that any exception can occur; no deduction whenever the answer affirms an exception in at least one scenario, regardless of mistaken claims about other scenarios.
2b:
**Sub-item 2b — "incorrectly states that a NullPointerException can occur here" (deduct 2):**

Deduct 2 points whenever the answer endorses a null-related failure as something that can happen in connection with this code, in any wording and at any point in the code path. This includes naming NullPointerException explicitly as a concrete additional candidate even when it is pinned on an unrelated or incidental cause (e.g. "Other potential exceptions include NullPointerException if system services are unavailable"), and it includes attributing the failure to a downstream consequence rather than the lookup-and-cast step itself — dereferencing the returned listener, later use of the fragment reference, or the caller receiving null. Informal phrasing counts the same as the exact exception name: "null pointer error", "null dereference crash", or "it will blow up on null" are all treated as claiming a NullPointerException and earn the deduction.

Do not deduct when the answer mentions NullPointerException only to reject it — e.g. "this is not an NPE — the null is cast, so it is a ClassCastException", or "NPE does not occur because casting null is legal." Mentioning the exception in order to rule it out is not an endorsement. Likewise, do not deduct for an unnamed, generic hedge about "other runtime exceptions" that never asserts a null-related failure for this code; the deduction under this sub-item requires an affirmative null/NPE claim, whether named or informally worded.
2c:
**Sub-item 2c — "If the answer incorrectly states that an IllegalStateException can occur here, 2 points should be deducted."**

Apply this deduction based on *where* the answer locates the IllegalStateException, not merely on whether the exception name appears. Deduct 2 points only if the answer attributes an IllegalStateException to the fragment-lookup/cast location being asked about — i.e., it presents an IllegalStateException as a possible outcome of looking up the fragment and casting it to `OnKeyListenerForFragments`. Do not deduct if the answer mentions IllegalStateException only in connection with clearly different code or context, such as committing a fragment transaction after `onSaveInstanceState`, or accessing the `FragmentManager` after the activity has been destroyed; in those cases the claim is not about the asked location and this sub-item is no_deduct.
2g:
**Sub-item 2g (other RuntimeException claimed) — grading note**

Deduct 2 points only when the answer names a concrete, incorrect exception class (e.g., "IndexOutOfBoundsException") *and* attributes it to the fragment lookup/cast location that the question is about — i.e., the answer claims that this specific code site can throw that named runtime exception. Both conditions must hold together for a deduction.

Do not deduct when the answer's wrong-type claim fails either condition. Specifically: if the answer attaches an incorrect exception type to some unrelated element elsewhere in the snippet rather than to the fragment lookup/cast, that is out of scope for 2g (it is handled by the location sub-item) and earns no deduction here. Likewise, vague or generic phrasing names no wrong type and earns no deduction — statements such as "this could throw a runtime exception," "an unchecked exception may be thrown," or "a crash/exception can occur" are not a claim of a specific incorrect exception class, even when made about the fragment lookup site.
4a:
**Sub-item 4a — "The answer should explain that if the fragment is not found, it will result in a ClassCastException" (1 point deduction if not mentioned).**

Award no deduction only when the answer explicitly names the absent/null return of `findFragmentById` as something that can go wrong at this line — i.e., it literally uses a missing/null token such as "or null", "returns null", "if no fragment is present", "no fragment found". A generic type-mismatch disjunction such as "or is not of the expected type" does **not** count; the wrong-type phrasing alone never satisfies this item. The not-found case does not have to be discussed separately: a combined sentence covering both cases (e.g., "if the returned fragment is missing or isn't an `OnKeyListenerForFragments`, you get a `ClassCastException`") earns credit here, and the same sentence may simultaneously satisfy the wrong-type item — but only because it contains the explicit missing/null reference alongside the wrong-type reference. Likewise, the exception the answer attributes to the not-found scenario is irrelevant here: as long as the answer raises the fragment-not-found/null case as a failure source, do not deduct even if it says a null result causes a `NullPointerException` or some other exception; mis-attribution is penalized by the incorrect-exception-type items, not by this mention check.

Deduct 1 point when the answer never names the missing/null return at all, or when it mentions null only to rule it out — e.g., it says `findFragmentById` never throws, or that a later null-check already protects against it, or otherwise presents the absence case as safe or impossible — since that affirmatively denies the not-found failure case rather than raising it.
